extraction_notes.note: The definitions of nonsingular bilinear map and tall tensor sit in the same sentences as cited results that Fact 3.1 restates; sentences cannot be split, so each whole sentence is one definition node and the restated results get no separate node.
Many results are justified only by a lead-in sentence ('By the first row expansion, we see the following'); these are zero-step prose proofs, some lacking a final period in the source.
\newtheorem{fact} environments state cited results, so they are theorems with origin external (Hard rule 4) rather than claims.
ClP7 keeps its two-sentence argument with the claim; AssumP2 includes the derived 'Then $u=m+n-2$.'; DP23 introduces both $N$ and the minor notation in one sentence.
Intro restatements of typical rank, the CGG/ten Berge/SMS results and the paper's main result are not separate nodes; the formal copies (Definition 2.1, Fact 3.1, Theorem 5.5) are kept.

nodes.name: d-tensor
nodes.statement: Precisely, let $N_1$, \ldots, $N_d$ be positive integers. A $d$-dimensional array datum $T=(t_{i_1\cdots i_d})_{1\leq i_j\leq N_j, 1\leq j\leq d}$ is called a $d$-way tensor or simply a $d$-tensor of format $N_1\times \cdots\times N_d$.

nodes.name: Tensor space notation
nodes.statement: For a set $S$, the set of $N_1\times \cdots\times N_d$ tensors with entries in $S$ is denoted by $S^{N_1\times \cdots\times N_d}$.

nodes.name: rank 1 tensor
nodes.statement: A non-zero tensor corresponding to an element of $V_1\otimes \cdots\otimes V_d$ of the form $\aaa_1\otimes\cdots\otimes \aaa_d$ is called a rank 1 tensor.
differentia: corresponding to an element of $V_1\otimes \cdots\otimes V_d$ of the form $\aaa_1\otimes\cdots\otimes \aaa_d$

nodes.name: Tensor rank
nodes.statement: For a general tensor $T$ of format $N_1\times\cdots\times N_d$, the rank of $T$, denoted by $\mathrm{rank} T$, is by definition the minimum integer $r$ such that $T$ can be expressed as a sum of $r$ rank 1 tensors, where we set the empty sum to be zero.
nodes.statement_short: The rank of a tensor is the minimum number of rank 1 tensors summing to it.

nodes.name: Chevalley's Theorem (Zariski open sets of bounded-rank tensors)
nodes.statement: If the base field is $\mathbb{C}$, the set of tensors of format $p\times n\times m$ with rank at most $r$ contains a non-empty Zariski open set if and only if its Zariski closure is $\mathbb{C}^{p\times n\times m}$ (cf., Chevalley's Theorem, see e.g., \cite[p.\ 39]{har92}).
conclusions: the set of tensors of format $p\times n\times m$ with rank at most $r$ contains a non-empty Zariski open set if and only if its Zariski closure is $\mathbb{C}^{p\times n\times m}$
nodes.statement_short: Over C, the bounded-rank locus contains a Zariski open set iff it is Zariski dense.

nodes.name: generic rank
nodes.statement: Therefore, there exists exactly one ``typical rank of $p\times n\times m$ tensors over $\mathbb{C}$''. This is called the generic rank of $p\times n\times m$ tensors over $\mathbb{C}$ and denoted as ${\mathrm{grank}}_\mathbb{C}(p,n,m)$ or simply ${\mathrm{grank}}(p,n,m)$.
nodes.statement_short: Over C there is a unique typical rank, the generic rank grank(p,n,m).

nodes.name: Generic rank equals minimal typical rank
nodes.statement: It is fairly easy to show that ${\mathrm{grank}}(p,n,m)=\min{\mathrm{trank}}(p,n,m)$ (see e.g., \cite[Chapter 6]{ssm16}).

nodes.name: Secant variety criterion for generic rank
nodes.statement: Further $r\geq {\mathrm{grank}}(p,n,m)$ if and only if the $r$-th higher secant variety of the image of Segre embedding $\mathbb{P}_\mathbb{C}\mathbb{C}^p\times\mathbb{P}_\mathbb{C}\mathbb{C}^n\times\mathbb{P}_\mathbb{C}\mathbb{C}^m \to\mathbb{P}_\mathbb{C}\mathbb{C}^{p\times n\times m}$ is the whole space $\mathbb{P}_\mathbb{C}\mathbb{C}^{p\times n\times m}$, where $\mathbb{P}_K V$ denotes the projective space consisting of one dimensional subspaces of the $K$-vector space $V$.
conclusions: $r\geq {\mathrm{grank}}(p,n,m)$ if and only if the $r$-th higher secant variety of the image of Segre embedding $\mathbb{P}_\mathbb{C}\mathbb{C}^p\times\mathbb{P}_\mathbb{C}\mathbb{C}^n\times\mathbb{P}_\mathbb{C}\mathbb{C}^m \to\mathbb{P}_\mathbb{C}\mathbb{C}^{p\times n\times m}$ is the whole space $\mathbb{P}_\mathbb{C}\mathbb{C}^{p\times n\times m}$
nodes.statement_short: grank is at most r iff the r-th secant variety of the Segre variety fills the ambient space.

nodes.name: Dimension-count lower bound on generic rank
nodes.statement: Thus, by counting the dimensions, we see that ${\mathrm{grank}}(p,n,m)\geq\lceil \frac{mnp}{m+n+p-2}\rceil$.

nodes.name: Threshold for the expected generic rank to be p
nodes.statement: Suppose that $3\leq m\leq n\leq p$. Then $p\geq\lceil\frac{mnp}{m+n+p-2}\rceil$ if and only if $p\geq(m-1)(n-1)+1$.

nodes.name: tall tensor
nodes.statement: ten Berge \cite{tb00} called a $p\times n\times m$-tensor with $(m-1)n<p<mn$ a tall array or a tall tensor and proved that ${\mathrm{trank}}(p,n,m)=\{p\}$ for these cases (see \cite[Chapter 6]{ssm16} for another proof).

nodes.name: semi-tall tensor
nodes.statement: Here we define a $p\times n\times m$-tensor a semi-tall tensor if $(m-1)(n-1)+1\leq p\leq (m-1)n$.

nodes.name: nonsingular bilinear map
nodes.statement: We \cite{ssm13,sms15,sms17} studied the plurality of typical ranks of semi-tall tensors and proved that if $(m-1)(n-1)+2\leq p\leq (m-1)n$, then ${\mathrm{trank}}(p,n,m)=\{p,p+1\}$ if there exists a nonsingular\ bilinear map $\mathbb{R}^m\times \mathbb{R}^n\to \mathbb{R}^{mn-p}$ and ${\mathrm{trank}}(p,n,m)=\{p\}$ otherwise, where a bilinear map $\varphi\colon V_1\times V_2\to W$ is nonsingular\ if $\varphi(x,y)=0$ implies $x=0$ or $y=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Prior results on semi-tall tensors with p >= (m-1)(n-1)+2, ending with the definition of a nonsingular bilinear map.

nodes.name: Slice notation for 3-tensors
nodes.statement: For $1\leq k\leq n$, we set $T_k=(t_{ijk})\in K^{\ell\times m}$ and denote $T=(T_1;\cdots;T_n)$.

nodes.name: Action of GL on tensors
nodes.statement: For $P\in {\mathrm{GL}}(\ell,K)$ and $Q\in {\mathrm{GL}}(m,K)$, we set $PTQ=(PT_1Q;\cdots;PT_nQ)$.

nodes.name: Rank invariance under GL action
nodes.statement: Note $\mathrm{rank} PTQ=\mathrm{rank} T$ by the definition of rank.

nodes.name: typical rank
nodes.statement: \rm If the set of rank $r$ tensors over $\mathbb{R}$ of format $\ell\times m\times n$ contains a non-empty Euclidean open subset of $\mathbb{R}^{\ell\times m\times n}$, then we say $r$ is a typical rank of $\ell\times m\times n$ tensors over $\mathbb{R}$. We denote the set of typical ranks of $\ell\times m\times n$ tensors over $\mathbb{R}$ by ${\mathrm{trank}}_\mathbb{R}(\ell,m,n)$ or simply ${\mathrm{trank}}(\ell,m,n)$.
differentia: the set of rank $r$ tensors over $\mathbb{R}$ of format $\ell\times m\times n$ contains a non-empty Euclidean open subset of $\mathbb{R}^{\ell\times m\times n}$
nodes.statement_short: r is a typical rank if rank-r real tensors contain a nonempty Euclidean open set; trank is the set of these.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.2
nodes.statement: By the definition of the rank, we see the following fact.
nodes.statement_short: Direct from the definition of rank (permuting tensor factors preserves rank).

nodes.name: Permutation invariance of typical ranks
nodes.statement: Let $n_1$, $n_2$ and $n_3$ be positive integers. Then ${\mathrm{trank}}(n_{i_1},n_{i_2},n_{i_3})={\mathrm{trank}}(n_1,n_2,n_3)$ for any permutation $i_1$, $i_2$, $i_3$ of 1, 2, 3.

nodes.name: flattenings
nodes.statement: \rm For $T=(T_1;\cdots;T_n)\in K^{\ell\times m\times n}$, we set $$ \mathrm{fl}_1(T)\mathrel{:=}(T_1,\ldots, T_n)\in K^{\ell\times mn} $$ and $$ \mathrm{fl}_2(T)\mathrel{:=} \begin{pmatrix}T_1\\\vdots\\T_n\end{pmatrix}\in K^{\ell n\times m} $$ and call flattenings of $T$.
nodes.statement_short: The two flattenings fl_1, fl_2 of a 3-tensor stack its slices horizontally or vertically.

nodes.name: Flattenings and rank
nodes.statement: By the correspondence $K^{\ell\times m\times n}\leftrightarrow V_1\otimes V_2\otimes V_3$, where $V_1$ (resp.\ $V_2$, $V_3$) is a vector space over $K$ of dimension $\ell$ (resp.\ $m$, $n$) with fixed basis, flattenings correspond to natural isomorphisms $V_1\otimes V_2\otimes V_3\to V_1\otimes (V_2\otimes V_3)$ and $V_1\otimes V_2\otimes V_3\to(V_1\otimes V_3)\otimes V_2$. In particular, $\mathrm{rank} (\mathrm{fl}_1(T))\leq \mathrm{rank} T$ and $\mathrm{rank}(\mathrm{fl}_2(T))\leq\mathrm{rank} T$.
nodes.statement_short: Flattenings are natural isomorphisms of tensor products, so their matrix ranks bound the tensor rank from below.

nodes.name: Row and column submatrix notation
nodes.statement: \rm For $M=(\mmm_1,\ldots,\mmm_n)= \begin{pmatrix}\mmm^{(1)}\\\vdots\\\mmm^{(\ell)}\end{pmatrix} \in K^{\ell\times n}$, we set $M_{\leq j}\mathrel{:=}(\mmm_1,\ldots, \mmm_{j})$, ${}_{j<}M\mathrel{:=}(\mmm_{j+1},\ldots, \mmm_{n})$, $M^{\leq i}\mathrel{:=}\begin{pmatrix}\mmm^{(1)}\\\vdots\\\mmm^{(i)}\end{pmatrix}$ and ${}^{i<}M\mathrel{:=}\begin{pmatrix}\mmm^{(i+1)}\\\vdots\\\mmm^{(\ell)}\end{pmatrix}$.
nodes.statement_short: Notation for the submatrices formed by the first j / last columns and first i / last rows.

nodes.name: Determinantal ideal
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $M\in R^{\ell\times n}$. We denote by $I_t(M)$ the ideal of $R$ generated by $t$-minors of $R$.

nodes.name: Standing assumption on m, n, p
nodes.statement: From now on, let $m$, $n$ and $p$ be integers with $3\leq m\leq n$ and $(m-1)(n-1)+1\leq p\leq mn$.
nodes.section: 3 A condition of an $n\times p\times m$-tensor to be of rank $p$

nodes.name: u = mn - p
nodes.statement: We set $u=mn-p$.
nodes.section: 3 A condition of an $n\times p\times m$-tensor to be of rank $p$

nodes.name: Known typical ranks of semi-tall and tall tensors
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item ${\mathrm{grank}}(p,n,m)=p$. In particular, $\min{\mathrm{trank}}(p,n,m)=p$ \cite{cgg02}. \item If $p>(m-1)n$, then ${\mathrm{trank}}(p,n,m)=\{p\}$ \cite{tb00}. \item Suppose $p\leq (m-1)n$. If there exists a nonsingular\ bilinear map $\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^u$, then ${\mathrm{trank}}(p,n,m)=\{p,p+1\}$. Moreover, if $(m-1)(n-1)+2\leq p$, then the converse also hold true \cite{ssm13,sms15, sms17}. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 3 A condition of an $n\times p\times m$-tensor to be of rank $p$
nodes.origin_citation: Catalisano, Geramita, Gimigliano 2002; ten Berge 2000; Sumi, Miyazaki, Sakata 2013, 2015, 2017
assumptions: If there exists a nonsingular\ bilinear map $\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^u$
nodes.statement_short: grank = p; tall tensors have the single typical rank p; semi-tall tensors have typical ranks {p,p+1} iff a nonsingular bilinear map exists (for p >= (m-1)(n-1)+2).

nodes.name: Semi-tall case p=(m-1)(n-1)+1 without nonsingular bilinear map
nodes.statement: Therefore, the case where $p=(m-1)(n-1)+1$ and there is no nonsingular\ bilinear map $\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^u$ is still left open.
nodes.section: 3 A condition of an $n\times p\times m$-tensor to be of rank $p$
nodes.statement_short: Determine trank when p=(m-1)(n-1)+1 and no nonsingular bilinear map R^m x R^n -> R^u exists.

nodes.name: trank(p,n,m)=trank(n,p,m)
nodes.statement: Note that ${\mathrm{trank}}(p,n,m)={\mathrm{trank}}(n,p,m)$.

nodes.name: Maps sigma, nu, tau, mu
nodes.statement: \rm We set $\mathscr{V}\mathrel{:=}\{T\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p\times m}\mid \mathrm{fl}_2(T)^{\leq p}$ is nonsingular.$\}$, $\mathscr{O}\mathrel{:=}\{Y\in\mathbb{R}^{u\times n\times m}\mid {}_{p<}\mathrm{fl}_1(Y)$ is nonsingular.$\}$, $\sigma\colon\mathscr{V}\to\mathbb{R}^{u\times p}$, $\sigma(T)=({}^{p<}\mathrm{fl}_2(T))(\mathrm{fl}_2(T)^{\leq p})^{-1}$, $\nu\colon\mathscr{O}\to\mathbb{R}^{u\times p}$, $\nu(Y)=-({}_{p<}\mathrm{fl}_1(Y))^{-1}(\mathrm{fl}_1(Y)_{\leq p})$, $\tau\colon\mathbb{R}^{u\times p}\to\mathscr{V}$, $\tau(W)=\mathrm{fl}_2^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}E_p\\ W\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mu\colon\mathbb{R}^{u\times p}\to\mathscr{O}$, $\mu(W)=\mathrm{fl}_1^{-1}(W,-E_u)$.
nodes.section: 3 A condition of an $n\times p\times m$-tensor to be of rank $p$
nodes.statement_short: Open sets V, O of tensors and maps sigma, nu to u x p matrices with sections tau, mu, built from flattenings.

nodes.name: Matrix pencil M(x,A)
nodes.statement: \rm Let $\xxx=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)$ be a row vector of indeterminates, i.e., $x_1$, \ldots, $x_m$ are independent indeterminates. For $A=(A_1;\cdots;A_m)\in\mathbb{R}^{u\times n\times m}$, we set $M(\xxx,A)\mathrel{:=} x_1A_1+\cdots+x_mA_m\in \mathbb{R}[x_1, \ldots, x_m]^{u\times n}$.
nodes.section: 3 A condition of an $n\times p\times m$-tensor to be of rank $p$

nodes.name: psi(a,b) and subspace U(Y)
nodes.statement: \rm Let $\aaa$ and $\bbb$ be column vectors with entries in $\mathbb{R}$ of dimension $m$ and $n$ respectively. We set $\psi(\aaa,\bbb)\mathrel{:=}(\aaa\otimes_\mathrm{Kr}\bbb)^{\leq p}$, where $\otimes_\mathrm{Kr}$ denotes the Kronecker product, i.e., if $\aaa=\begin{pmatrix}a_1\\\vdots\\ a_m\end{pmatrix}$, then $\psi(\aaa,\bbb)= \begin{pmatrix}a_1\bbb\\\vdots\\ a_{m-2}\bbb\\ a_{m-1}\bbb^{\leq p-(m-2)n}\end{pmatrix}$. For $Y\in\mathbb{R}^{u\times n\times m}$, we define $U(Y)$ to be the vector subspace of $\mathbb{R}^p$ generated by $\{\psi(\aaa,\bbb)\mid M(\aaa^\top,Y)\bbb=\zerovec\}$.
nodes.section: 3 A condition of an $n\times p\times m$-tensor to be of rank $p$
nodes.statement_short: psi(a,b) is the first p entries of the Kronecker product; U(Y) is spanned by psi(a,b) over kernel pairs of M(a^T,Y).

nodes.name: Rank-p criterion via dim U
nodes.statement: For $T\in\mathscr{V}$, $\mathrm{rank} T=p$ if and only if $\dim U(\mu(\sigma(T)))=p$.
nodes.section: 3 A condition of an $n\times p\times m$-tensor to be of rank $p$
conclusions: $\mathrm{rank} T=p$ if and only if $\dim U(\mu(\sigma(T)))=p$.
nodes.statement_short: A tensor T in V has rank p iff the subspace U(mu(sigma(T))) is all of R^p.
nodes.label: lem:rank p

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.6
nodes.statement: Set $\mu(\sigma(T))=W=(W_1;\cdots;W_m)$ and $\ell=u-n$. Then by \cite[Theorem 6.5 (1)$\iff$(3)]{sms17}, we see that $\mathrm{rank} T=p$ if and only if there are $B=(\bbb_1, \ldots, \bbb_p)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$ and $p\times p$ diagonal matrices $D_1$, \ldots, $D_m$ such that $$ (\ast) \left\{ \begin{array}{lll} D_k=\mathrm{Diag}(d_{1k},\ldots, d_{pk})&\mbox{for $1\leq k\leq m$,}\\ (d_{j1}W_1+\cdots+d_{jm}W_m)\bbb_j=\zerovec&\mbox{for $1\leq j\leq p$ and}\\ \mbox{$\begin{pmatrix} BD_1\\\vdots\\BD_{m-2}\\B^{\leq n-\ell}D_{m-1}\end{pmatrix}$ is nonsingular.} \end{array} \right. $$ First suppose that there are $B=(\bbb_1, \ldots, \bbb_p)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$ and $D_1$, \ldots, $D_m$ which satisfy $(\ast)$. If we set $\aaa_j=(d_{j1},\ldots, d_{jm})^\top$ for $1\leq j\leq p$, then $$ M(\aaa_j^\top,W)\bbb_j=\zerovec $$ for $1\leq j\leq p$ and $$ (\psi(\aaa_1,\bbb_1), \ldots,\psi(\aaa_p,\bbb_p))= \begin{pmatrix} BD_1\\\vdots\\BD_{m-2}\\B^{\leq n-\ell}D_{m-1}\end{pmatrix} $$ is nonsingular. Therefore $\dim U(\mu(\sigma(T)))=p$. Conversely, assume that $\dim U(\mu(\sigma(T)))=p$. Then there are $\aaa_1$, \ldots, $\aaa_p\in\mathbb{R}^m$ and $\bbb_1$, \ldots, $\bbb_p\in\mathbb{R}^n$ such that $\psi(\aaa_1,\bbb_1)$, \ldots, $\psi(\aaa_p,\bbb_p)$ are linearly independent. Set $\aaa_j=(d_{j1},\ldots,d_{jm})^\top$ for $1\leq j\leq p$, $D_k=\mathrm{Diag}(d_{1k},\ldots,d_{pk})$ for $1\leq k\leq m$ and $B=(\bbb_1,\ldots,\bbb_p)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$. Then it is easily verified that $B$ and $D_1$, \ldots, $D_m$ satisfy $(\ast)$.
nodes.section: 3 A condition of an $n\times p\times m$-tensor to be of rank $p$
nodes.statement_short: Reduce via a cited rank-p criterion (diagonal matrices D_k and B) and show each direction by translating between (*) and spanning vectors psi(a_j,b_j).

nodes.name: Case p=(m-1)(n-1)+1
nodes.statement: From now on, we consider the case where $p=(m-1)(n-1)+1$. Then $u=m+n-2$.

nodes.name: Special tensor A
nodes.statement: \rm We set $$ A_k\mathrel{:=}\begin{pmatrix}O_{(k-1)\times n}\\ E_n\\ O_{(m-k-1)\times n}\end{pmatrix} \in\mathbb{R}^{u\times n} $$ for $1\leq k\leq m-1$ and $$ A_{m}\mathrel{:=}\begin{pmatrix}O_{(m-1)\times(n-1)}&-\eee_1\\ E_{n-1}&\zerovec\end{pmatrix} \in\mathbb{R}^{u\times n}, $$ where $\eee_1=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\\vdots\\0\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{m-1}$ and $A=(A_1;\cdots;A_m)\in\mathbb{R}^{u\times n\times m}$.
nodes.statement_short: An explicit u x n x m tensor A built from identity blocks and a shifted block with -e_1.

nodes.name: Key lemma: determinantal points and factors of y^u+1
nodes.statement: Let $y$ be an indeterminate and $a_1,\ldots, a_{m-1}\in\mathbb{C}$. Then the following conditions are equivalent, where $V_a(I)$ denotes the affine variety defined by an ideal $I$. \begin{enumerate} \item $(a_1,\ldots, a_{m-1},-1)\in V_a(I_n(M(\xxx,A)))$. \item $y^{m-1}-a_{m-1}y^{m-2}-\cdots-a_2y-a_1$ is a factor of $y^u+1$. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: Let $y$ be an indeterminate and $a_1,\ldots, a_{m-1}\in\mathbb{C}$.
nodes.statement_short: Points of the determinantal variety of M(x,A) with last coordinate -1 correspond to monic degree-(m-1) factors of y^u+1.
nodes.label: lem:key

nodes.name: Annihilator ideal of a sequence
nodes.statement: \rm Let $y$ be an indeterminate and $\{\mu_t\}_{t\geq 1}$ an infinite sequence of complex numbers. We set $\mathscr{I}(\{\mu_t\}_{t\geq 1}) =\{f(y)\in\mathbb{C}[y]\mid f(y)=\sum_k c_k y^k$, $\sum_k c_k\mu_{k+t}=0$ for any $t\geq 1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Polynomials whose coefficients give a linear recurrence satisfied by the sequence.

nodes.name: I(mu) is an ideal
nodes.statement: It is easily verified that $\mathscr{I}(\{\mu_t\}_{t\geq 1})$ is an ideal of $\mathbb{C}[y]$.

nodes.name: Sequence lambda_t
nodes.statement: Now let $a_1$, \ldots, $a_{m-1}\in\mathbb{C}$. Set $\lambda_t=0$ for $1\leq t\leq m-2$, $\lambda_{m-1}=1$ and $$ \lambda_{m-1+s}= \det\begin{pmatrix} a_{m-1}&a_{m-2}&\cdots&a_1\\ -1&\ddots&\ddots&&\ddots\\ &\ddots&\ddots&\ddots&&a_1\\ &&\ddots&\ddots&\ddots&\vdots\\ &&&\ddots&\ddots&a_{m-2}\\ &&&&-1&a_{m-1} \end{pmatrix} $$ for $s\geq 1$, where the right hand side is an $s\times s$-determinant (some $a_i$'s may not appear for small $s$).
nodes.statement_short: lambda_t: m-2 zeros, then 1, then s x s Hessenberg determinants in the a_i.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.4
nodes.statement: By the first row expansion, we see the following
nodes.statement_short: First row expansion of the defining determinants.

nodes.name: Recurrence for lambda_t
nodes.statement: For $t\geq m$, we have $\lambda_t=\sum_{k=1}^{m-1}a_{m-k}\lambda_{t-k}$.
nodes.label: lem:rec rel

nodes.name: I(lambda) is generated by h(y)
nodes.statement: By the above lemma, we see that $h(y)\in\mathscr{I}(\{\lambda_t\}_{t\geq 1})$. Further, since $\lambda_t=0$ for $1\leq t\leq m-2$ and $\lambda_{m-1}=1$, there is no polynomial in $\mathscr{I}(\{\lambda_t\}_{t\geq 1})$ whose degree is less than $m-1$ except the zero polynomial, i.e., $\mathscr{I}(\{\lambda_t\}_{t\geq 1})$ is generated by $h(y)$.
nodes.statement_short: h lies in the annihilator ideal of lambda, and since no lower-degree polynomial does, h generates it.

nodes.name: Matrix N and maximal minors
nodes.statement: Set $$ N=M((a_1,\ldots, a_{m-1},-1),A) =\begin{pmatrix}a_1&&&&1\\ a_2&\ddots\\ \vdots&\ddots&\ddots\\ a_{m-1}&&\ddots&\ddots\\ -1&\ddots&&\ddots&a_1\\ &\ddots&\ddots&&a_2\\ &&\ddots&\ddots&\vdots\\ &&&-1&a_{m-1} \end{pmatrix} $$ and for integers $c_1$, \ldots, $c_n$ with $1\leq c_1<\cdots<c_n\leq u$, we denote by $[c_1, \ldots, c_n]_N$ the maximal minor of $N$ consisting of the $c_1$-th, \ldots, $c_n$-th rows of $N$.
nodes.statement_short: N is the pencil M(x,A) evaluated at (a_1,...,a_{m-1},-1); [c_1..c_n]_N denotes its maximal minors.

nodes.name: Rank-deficiency criterion for N
nodes.statement: Under the notation above, the following conditions are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item $\mathrm{rank} N<n$. \item $[i,m,m+1,\ldots,u]_N=0$ for $1\leq i\leq m-1$. \item $\lambda_{u+t}=0$ for $1\leq t\leq m-2$ and $\lambda_{u+m-1}=-1$. \item $\lambda_{u+t}=-\lambda_t$ for $t\geq 1$. \item $y^u+1\in\mathscr{I}(\{\lambda_t\}_{t\geq 1})$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: rank N < n iff certain maximal minors vanish iff lambda satisfies lambda_{u+t} = -lambda_t iff y^u+1 annihilates lambda.
nodes.label: lem:non full rank

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.5
nodes.statement: Let $$ U=\begin{pmatrix} a_{m-1}&a_{m-2}&\cdots&a_1&&1\\ -1&\ddots&\ddots&&\ddots\\ &\ddots&\ddots&\ddots&&a_1\\ &&\ddots&\ddots&\ddots&\vdots\\ &&&\ddots&\ddots&a_{m-2}\\ &&&&-1&a_{m-1} \end{pmatrix} $$ be a $u\times u$ matrix. Then $\det({}^{t<}_{t<}U)=\lambda_{u+m-1-t}+\delta_{0,t}$ for $0\leq t\leq u-1$, where $\delta_{0,t}$ is the Kronecker's delta. \ref{item:rank less than n}$\Longrightarrow$\ref{item:lambda u+1}: Since ${}_{m-2<}U=N$ and $\mathrm{rank} N<n$ by assumption, we see that $\det({}^{t<}_{t<}U)=0$ for $0\leq t\leq m-2$. Thus, we see that $\lambda_{u+m-1-t}+\delta_{0,t}=0$ for $0\leq t\leq m-2$. \ref{item:lambda u+1}$\Longrightarrow$\ref{item:minors vanish}: We see by the first row expansions of $\det({}_{t<}^{t<}U)$ and $[t+1,m,\ldots, u]$ and the assumption that \begin{eqnarray*} 0&=&\lambda_{u+m-1-t}+\delta_{0,t}\\ &=&\sum_{k=1}^{m-1}a_{m-k}\lambda_{u+m-1-t-k}+\delta_{0,t}\\ &=&\sum_{k=m-t-1}^{m-1}a_{m-k}\lambda_{u+m-1-t-k}+\delta_{0,t}\\ &=&\sum_{s=1}^{t+1}a_{t+2-s}\lambda_{u+1-s}+\delta_{0,t}\\ &=&[t+1,m,\ldots, u]_N \end{eqnarray*} for $0\leq t\leq m-2$. \ref{item:minors vanish}$\Longrightarrow$\ref{item:rank less than n} follows from the fact that the last $n-1$ rows of $N$ are linearly independent, \ref{item:lambda u+1}$\iff$\ref{item:rec u} follows from the facts that $\lambda_1=\cdots=\lambda_{m-2}=0$ and $\lambda_{m-1}=1$ and Lemma \ref{lem:rec rel} and \ref{item:rec u}$\iff$\ref{item:yu} follows from the definition of $\mathscr{I}(\{\lambda_t\}_{t\geq 1})$.
nodes.statement_short: Embed N in a u x u Hessenberg matrix U whose trailing principal minors are lambda values; chain the implications via row expansions and the recurrence.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.2
nodes.statement: Since $(a_1,\ldots, a_{m-1},-1)\in V_a(I_n(M(\xxx,A)))$ if and only if $\mathrm{rank} N<n$ and $y^u+1\in\mathscr{I}(\{\lambda_t\}_{t\geq 1})$ if and only if $h(y)$ divides $y^u+1$, we see Lemma \ref{lem:key} by Lemma \ref{lem:non full rank}.
nodes.statement_short: Combine Lemma 4.5 with the fact that the annihilator ideal is generated by h(y).

nodes.name: Degree and codimension of the maximal-minor determinantal variety
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a $u\times n$ matrix of indeterminates. Then the projective variety in $\mathbb{P}_\mathbb{C}\mathbb{C}^{u\times n}$ defined by $I_n(X)$ has degree ${u\choose n-1}$ and codimension $u-n+1$.
assumptions: Let $X$ be a $u\times n$ matrix of indeterminates.
conclusions: the projective variety in $\mathbb{P}_\mathbb{C}\mathbb{C}^{u\times n}$ defined by $I_n(X)$ has degree ${u\choose n-1}$ and codimension $u-n+1$.
nodes.label: fac:deg

nodes.name: Binomial identities for u=m+n-2
nodes.statement: Note that ${u\choose n-1}={u\choose m-1}$ and $u-n+1=m-1$ since $u=m+n-2$.

nodes.name: Number of monic degree-(m-1) factors of y^u+1
nodes.statement: Note also that there are ${u\choose m-1}$ monic factors of $y^u+1$ of degree $m-1$ in $\mathbb{C}[y]$.
conclusions: there are ${u\choose m-1}$ monic factors of $y^u+1$ of degree $m-1$ in $\mathbb{C}[y]$

nodes.name: Linear map phi_B
nodes.statement: \rm For $B=(B_1;\cdots; B_m)\in\mathbb{C}^{u\times n\times m}$, we set $\varphi_B\colon\mathbb{C}^m\to\mathbb{C}^{u\times n}$, $(\alpha_1,\ldots, \alpha_m)\mapsto\alpha_1B_1+\cdots+\alpha_mB_m$.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 4.8
nodes.statement: Then by Lemma \ref{lem:key}, Fact \ref{fac:deg} and Bezout's theorem, we see the following
nodes.statement_short: Bezout's theorem: the key lemma gives u choose (m-1) intersection points, matching the degree of the determinantal variety.

nodes.name: Transverse intersection of Im(phi_A) with the determinantal variety
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbb{P}_\mathbb{C}({\mathrm{Im}}\varphi_A)$ be the linear subspace of $\mathbb{P}_\mathbb{C}\mathbb{C}^{u\times n}$ defined by ${\mathrm{Im}}\varphi_A$. Then $\mathbb{P}_\mathbb{C}({\mathrm{Im}}\varphi_A)$ and $V_p(I_n(X))$ intersect transversely at ${u\choose m-1}$ distinct points, where $V_p(I)$ denotes the projective variety defined by the homogeneous ideal $I$.
assumptions: Let $\mathbb{P}_\mathbb{C}({\mathrm{Im}}\varphi_A)$ be the linear subspace of $\mathbb{P}_\mathbb{C}\mathbb{C}^{u\times n}$ defined by ${\mathrm{Im}}\varphi_A$.
conclusions: $\mathbb{P}_\mathbb{C}({\mathrm{Im}}\varphi_A)$ and $V_p(I_n(X))$ intersect transversely at ${u\choose m-1}$ distinct points

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 4.9
nodes.statement: By the implicit function theorem, we see the following fact.
nodes.statement_short: Implicit function theorem: transverse intersection points persist and stay real/non-real under small perturbation.

nodes.name: Stable count of real points near A
nodes.statement: There is a Euclidean open neighborhood $\mathscr{U}$ of $A$ in $\mathbb{R}^{u\times n\times m}$ such that if $B\in\mathscr{U}$, then $\varphi_B$ is injective and the number of real points of $V_p(I_n(M(\xxx,B)))\subset\mathbb{P}_\mathbb{C}\mathbb{C}^m$ is the number of real monic polynomials of degree $m-1$ which divide $y^u+1$, where we say a point of a complex projective space is real if all possible ratios of its homogeneous coordintes are real numbers.
conclusions: the number of real points of $V_p(I_n(M(\xxx,B)))\subset\mathbb{P}_\mathbb{C}\mathbb{C}^m$ is the number of real monic polynomials of degree $m-1$ which divide $y^u+1$
nodes.statement_short: Near A, the real points of the determinantal variety of M(x,B) are counted by real monic degree-(m-1) divisors of y^u+1.

nodes.name: alpha(m,n)
nodes.statement: We denote the number of real monic polynomials of degree $m-1$ which divides $y^u+1$ by $\alpha(m,n)$.

nodes.name: Formula for alpha(m,n)
nodes.statement: $$ \alpha(m,n)= \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} {u/2\choose (m-1)/2}&\quad\mbox{if $m$ and $n$ are odd,}\\ {(u-1)/2\choose (m-2)/2}&\quad\mbox{if $m$ is even and $n$ is odd,}\\ {(u-1)/2\choose (m-1)/2}&\quad\mbox{if $m$ is odd and $n$ is even and}\\ 0&\quad\mbox{if $m$ and $n$ are even.} \end{array} \right. $$
conclusions: $$ \alpha(m,n)= \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} {u/2\choose (m-1)/2}&\quad\mbox{if $m$ and $n$ are odd,}\\ {(u-1)/2\choose (m-2)/2}&\quad\mbox{if $m$ is even and $n$ is odd,}\\ {(u-1)/2\choose (m-1)/2}&\quad\mbox{if $m$ is odd and $n$ is even and}\\ 0&\quad\mbox{if $m$ and $n$ are even.} \end{array} \right. $$
nodes.statement_short: alpha(m,n) is a binomial coefficient depending on parities of m and n, and 0 when both are even.
nodes.label: lem:alpha m n

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.11
nodes.statement: By replacing $\mathscr{U}$ to a smaller neighborhood if necessary, we may assume that $\mathrm{rank} (M(\aaa,B)_{\leq n-1})=n-1$ for any $B\in\mathscr{U}$ and $\aaa\in\mathbb{R}^m\setminus\{\zerovec\}$ (cf.\ \cite[Corollary 4.20]{sms17}). Then we have the following fact.
nodes.statement_short: Shrink the neighborhood so the first n-1 columns of M(a,B) have full rank, making kernel vectors unique up to scale.

nodes.name: Count of real psi-points for B near A
nodes.statement: Suppose $B\in\mathscr{U}$. Then $\#\{[\psi(\aaa,\bbb)]\in\mathbb{P}_\mathbb{R}\mathbb{R}^p\mid M(\aaa,B)\bbb=\zerovec, \aaa\in\mathbb{R}^m\setminus\{\zerovec\}, \bbb\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{\zerovec\}\} =\alpha(m,n)$, where $[\xxx]$ denotes the point of $\mathbb{P}_\mathbb{R}\mathbb{R}^p$ defined by $\xxx\in\mathbb{R}^p\setminus\{\zerovec\}$.
nodes.label: lem:number gen

nodes.name: Plural typical ranks when m-1 and n-1 are not bit-disjoint
nodes.statement: If $m-1$ and $n-1$ are not bit-disjoint, then ${\mathrm{trank}}(n,p,m)=\{p,p+1\}$, where two positive integers are bit-disjoint if there are no 1's in the same place of their binary notation.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors
nodes.label: fact:bit dis

nodes.name: Known formats with typical ranks {p,p+1}
nodes.statement: \rm ${\mathrm{trank}}(n,p,m)=\{p,p+1\}$ in the following cases. \begin{enumerate} \item Both $m$ and $n$ are even. \item $m=5$ and $n\equiv 5,6,7,8\pmod 8$. \item $m=6$ and $n\equiv 2,4,5,6,7,8\pmod 8$. \item $m=7$ and $n\equiv 3,4,5,6,7,8\pmod 8$. \item $m=8$ and $n\equiv 2,3,4,5,6,7,8\pmod 8$. \item $m=9$ and $n\equiv 9,10,11,12,13,14,15,16\pmod {16}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors
nodes.statement_short: Formats (m,n) where m-1, n-1 are not bit-disjoint, so trank = {p,p+1}.
nodes.label: ex:known

nodes.name: Tensor A''
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors

nodes.name: Permutation normalizing A''
nodes.statement: Then there is a permutation matrix $P\in{\mathrm{GL}}(u,\mathbb{R})$ such that ${}_{p<}\mathrm{fl}_1(PA'')=-E_u$.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors
conclusions: there is a permutation matrix $P\in{\mathrm{GL}}(u,\mathbb{R})$ such that ${}_{p<}\mathrm{fl}_1(PA'')=-E_u$

nodes.name: A' and W_0
nodes.statement: Set $A'=PA''$ and $W_0=\mathrm{fl}_1(A')_{\leq p}$.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors

nodes.name: Map rho and neighborhood calU
nodes.statement: Further set $\rho\colon\mathbb{R}^{u\times n\times m}\to\mathbb{R}^{u\times n\times m}$, $B=(B_1;\cdots;B_m)\mapsto P(B_2;\cdots;B_{m-2};B_m;-B_{m-1};-B_{1})$ and ${\mathcal U}=\mu^{-1}(\rho(\mathscr{U}))$, where $\mu$ is the map defined in Definition \ref{def:sigma nu}.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors
nodes.statement_short: rho permutes and signs the slices of a tensor; calU is the preimage under mu of rho(scrU).

nodes.name: calU is an open neighborhood of W_0
nodes.statement: Then ${\mathcal U}$ is an open neighborhood of $W_0$.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors
conclusions: ${\mathcal U}$ is an open neighborhood of $W_0$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.3
nodes.statement: Further, we see the following fact by Lemma \ref{lem:number gen}.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors
nodes.statement_short: Transport Lemma 4.11 through the maps rho and mu.

nodes.name: Count of real psi-points on sigma^{-1}(calU)
nodes.statement: If $T\in\sigma^{-1}({\mathcal U})$, then $\#\{[\psi(\aaa,\bbb)]\in\mathbb{P}_\mathbb{R}\mathbb{R}^p\mid M(\aaa,\mu(\sigma(T)))\bbb=\zerovec, \aaa\in\mathbb{R}^m\setminus\{\zerovec\}, \bbb\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{\zerovec\}\} =\alpha(m,n)$.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.4
nodes.statement: Since $\sigma^{-1}({\mathcal U})$ contains $\tau(W_0)$, $\sigma^{-1}({\mathcal U})$ is not an empty set. Therefore, we see by Lemma \ref{lem:rank p} that if $\alpha(m,n)<p$, then there exists a non-empty Euclidean open subset $\sigma^{-1}({\mathcal U})$ of $\mathbb{R}^{n\times p\times m}$ consisting of tensors of rank larger than $p$. Further, since we see by \cite[Theorem 8.1]{sms17} that typical ranks of $n\times p\times m$ tensors are less than or equal to $p+1$, we see the following fact.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 5.3 and Lemma 3.6 give a nonempty open set of tensors of rank > p when alpha(m,n) < p; a cited bound caps typical ranks at p+1.

nodes.name: alpha(m,n) < p implies plural typical ranks
nodes.statement: If $\alpha(m,n)<p$, then ${\mathrm{trank}}(n,p,m)=\{p,p+1\}$.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors
nodes.label: lem:less than p

nodes.name: Main theorem: typical ranks {p,p+1} for p=(m-1)(n-1)+1
nodes.statement: Suppose $3\leq m\leq n$ and $p=(m-1)(n-1)+1$. Then ${\mathrm{trank}}(n,p,m)=\{p,p+1\}$ in the following cases. \begin{enumerate} \item $m=3$ or $m=4$. \item $m=5$ and $n\leq 26$ or $n=28$. \item $m=6$ and $n\leq 34$. \item $m=7$ and $n\leq 16$. \item $m=8$ and $n\leq 16$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors
nodes.statement_short: For p=(m-1)(n-1)+1, trank(n,p,m)={p,p+1} for m=3,4, and listed ranges of n for m=5,...,8.
nodes.label: thm:main

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5.5
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:alpha m n} and computation, we see that $\alpha(m,n)<p$ in the following cases: (1) $m=3$ or $m=4$, (2) $m=5$ and $n\leq 26$ or $n=28$, (3) $m=6$ and $n\leq 34$, (4) $m=7$ and $n\leq 12$, (5) $m=8$ and $n\leq 14$ and (6) $m=9$ and $n=10$. Thus, we see the result by Example \ref{ex:known} and Lemma \ref{lem:less than p}.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors
nodes.statement_short: Compute alpha(m,n) from Lemma 4.10 and check alpha(m,n) < p case by case; cover remaining cases with Example 5.2.

nodes.name: Converse of the bit-disjointness criterion fails
nodes.statement: \rm Set $m=3$ and $n=5$. Then $m-1$ and $n-1$ are bit-disjoint. However, by Theorem \ref{thm:main}, we see that ${\mathrm{trank}}(n,p,m)=\{p,p+1\}$. Thus the converse of Fact \ref{fact:bit dis} does not valid.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors
nodes.statement_short: m=3, n=5 has bit-disjoint m-1, n-1 yet trank={p,p+1}, so the converse of Fact 5.1 fails.

nodes.name: Reduce to condition (*)
nodes.statement: Set $\mu(\sigma(T))=W=(W_1;\cdots;W_m)$ and $\ell=u-n$. Then by \cite[Theorem 6.5 (1)$\iff$(3)]{sms17}, we see that $\mathrm{rank} T=p$ if and only if there are $B=(\bbb_1, \ldots, \bbb_p)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$ and $p\times p$ diagonal matrices $D_1$, \ldots, $D_m$ such that $$ (\ast) \left\{ \begin{array}{lll} D_k=\mathrm{Diag}(d_{1k},\ldots, d_{pk})&\mbox{for $1\leq k\leq m$,}\\ (d_{j1}W_1+\cdots+d_{jm}W_m)\bbb_j=\zerovec&\mbox{for $1\leq j\leq p$ and}\\ \mbox{$\begin{pmatrix} BD_1\\\vdots\\BD_{m-2}\\B^{\leq n-\ell}D_{m-1}\end{pmatrix}$ is nonsingular.} \end{array} \right. $$
nodes.section: 3 A condition of an $n\times p\times m$-tensor to be of rank $p$
nodes.statement_short: Invoke a cited rank-p criterion: existence of B and diagonal D_k satisfying (*).

nodes.name: (*) implies dim U = p
nodes.statement: First suppose that there are $B=(\bbb_1, \ldots, \bbb_p)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$ and $D_1$, \ldots, $D_m$ which satisfy $(\ast)$. If we set $\aaa_j=(d_{j1},\ldots, d_{jm})^\top$ for $1\leq j\leq p$, then $$ M(\aaa_j^\top,W)\bbb_j=\zerovec $$ for $1\leq j\leq p$ and $$ (\psi(\aaa_1,\bbb_1), \ldots,\psi(\aaa_p,\bbb_p))= \begin{pmatrix} BD_1\\\vdots\\BD_{m-2}\\B^{\leq n-\ell}D_{m-1}\end{pmatrix} $$ is nonsingular. Therefore $\dim U(\mu(\sigma(T)))=p$.
nodes.section: 3 A condition of an $n\times p\times m$-tensor to be of rank $p$
nodes.statement_short: From (*) build p independent vectors psi(a_j,b_j) in U, so dim U = p.

nodes.name: dim U = p implies (*)
nodes.statement: Conversely, assume that $\dim U(\mu(\sigma(T)))=p$. Then there are $\aaa_1$, \ldots, $\aaa_p\in\mathbb{R}^m$ and $\bbb_1$, \ldots, $\bbb_p\in\mathbb{R}^n$ such that $\psi(\aaa_1,\bbb_1)$, \ldots, $\psi(\aaa_p,\bbb_p)$ are linearly independent. Set $\aaa_j=(d_{j1},\ldots,d_{jm})^\top$ for $1\leq j\leq p$, $D_k=\mathrm{Diag}(d_{1k},\ldots,d_{pk})$ for $1\leq k\leq m$ and $B=(\bbb_1,\ldots,\bbb_p)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$. Then it is easily verified that $B$ and $D_1$, \ldots, $D_m$ satisfy $(\ast)$.
nodes.section: 3 A condition of an $n\times p\times m$-tensor to be of rank $p$
nodes.statement_short: From p independent psi(a_j,b_j) read off B and D_k satisfying (*).

nodes.name: Auxiliary matrix U
nodes.statement: Let $$ U=\begin{pmatrix} a_{m-1}&a_{m-2}&\cdots&a_1&&1\\ -1&\ddots&\ddots&&\ddots\\ &\ddots&\ddots&\ddots&&a_1\\ &&\ddots&\ddots&\ddots&\vdots\\ &&&\ddots&\ddots&a_{m-2}\\ &&&&-1&a_{m-1} \end{pmatrix} $$ be a $u\times u$ matrix. Then $\det({}^{t<}_{t<}U)=\lambda_{u+m-1-t}+\delta_{0,t}$ for $0\leq t\leq u-1$, where $\delta_{0,t}$ is the Kronecker's delta.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the u x u matrix U and express its trailing principal minors via lambda.

nodes.name: (1) implies (3)
nodes.statement: \ref{item:rank less than n}$\Longrightarrow$\ref{item:lambda u+1}: Since ${}_{m-2<}U=N$ and $\mathrm{rank} N<n$ by assumption, we see that $\det({}^{t<}_{t<}U)=0$ for $0\leq t\leq m-2$. Thus, we see that $\lambda_{u+m-1-t}+\delta_{0,t}=0$ for $0\leq t\leq m-2$.
nodes.statement_short: Rank deficiency of N forces the minors of U, hence lambda values, to vanish.

nodes.name: (3) implies (2)
nodes.statement: \ref{item:lambda u+1}$\Longrightarrow$\ref{item:minors vanish}: We see by the first row expansions of $\det({}_{t<}^{t<}U)$ and $[t+1,m,\ldots, u]$ and the assumption that \begin{eqnarray*} 0&=&\lambda_{u+m-1-t}+\delta_{0,t}\\ &=&\sum_{k=1}^{m-1}a_{m-k}\lambda_{u+m-1-t-k}+\delta_{0,t}\\ &=&\sum_{k=m-t-1}^{m-1}a_{m-k}\lambda_{u+m-1-t-k}+\delta_{0,t}\\ &=&\sum_{s=1}^{t+1}a_{t+2-s}\lambda_{u+1-s}+\delta_{0,t}\\ &=&[t+1,m,\ldots, u]_N \end{eqnarray*} for $0\leq t\leq m-2$.
nodes.statement_short: First-row expansion turns the lambda conditions into vanishing of the maximal minors.

nodes.name: Remaining implications
nodes.statement: \ref{item:minors vanish}$\Longrightarrow$\ref{item:rank less than n} follows from the fact that the last $n-1$ rows of $N$ are linearly independent, \ref{item:lambda u+1}$\iff$\ref{item:rec u} follows from the facts that $\lambda_1=\cdots=\lambda_{m-2}=0$ and $\lambda_{m-1}=1$ and Lemma \ref{lem:rec rel} and \ref{item:rec u}$\iff$\ref{item:yu} follows from the definition of $\mathscr{I}(\{\lambda_t\}_{t\geq 1})$.
nodes.statement_short: Close the cycle of implications using independence of rows, the recurrence, and the definition of the ideal.

nodes.name: Nonemptiness
nodes.statement: Since $\sigma^{-1}({\mathcal U})$ contains $\tau(W_0)$, $\sigma^{-1}({\mathcal U})$ is not an empty set.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors
nodes.statement_short: sigma^{-1}(calU) contains tau(W_0), hence is nonempty.

nodes.name: Open set of rank > p
nodes.statement: Therefore, we see by Lemma \ref{lem:rank p} that if $\alpha(m,n)<p$, then there exists a non-empty Euclidean open subset $\sigma^{-1}({\mathcal U})$ of $\mathbb{R}^{n\times p\times m}$ consisting of tensors of rank larger than $p$.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 3.6 and Lemma 5.3, if alpha(m,n)<p, sigma^{-1}(calU) is an open set of tensors of rank > p.

nodes.name: Conclude with upper bound
nodes.statement: Further, since we see by \cite[Theorem 8.1]{sms17} that typical ranks of $n\times p\times m$ tensors are less than or equal to $p+1$, we see the following fact.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors
nodes.statement_short: Cited bound: typical ranks are at most p+1, so trank={p,p+1}.
